While the upper bound above is not difficult to show (Theorem 17; this may be viewed as an “exponential analogue” of Toda’s theorem), the lower bound is surprisingly subtle. The naive strategy of replacing each proof yi of QCPH with pure state proof |ψi ⟩, which is then measured in the standard basis, does not work, as the measurement gives rise to mixed states. Mixed states, in turn, are difficult to handle in QPH, as the latter is not a convex optimization due to alternating quantifiers. We remark that while QPH ⊆ pureQPH follows easily via purification of proofs, we do not know how to show the analogous lower bound QCPH ⊆ QPH (our approach uses our asymmetric product test, which requires pure states).

Upper and lower bounds on pureQPH. Having introduced pureQPH in this work, we next give bounds on its power. ▶ Theorem 4. QCPH ⊆ pureQPH ⊆ EXPPP . While the upper bound above is not difficult to show (Theorem 17; this may be viewed as an “exponential analogue” of Toda’s theorem), the lower bound is surprisingly subtle. The naive strategy of replacing each proof yi of QCPH with pure state proof |ψi ⟩, which is then measured in the standard basis, does not work, as the measurement gives rise to mixed states. Mixed states, in turn, are difficult to handle in QPH, as the latter is not a convex optimization due to alternating quantifiers. We remark that while QPH ⊆ pureQPH follows easily via purification of proofs, we do not know how to show the analogous lower bound QCPH ⊆ QPH (our approach uses our asymmetric product test, which requires pure states). 2 QMA(2) is QMA with two proofs in tensor product.
